claims.text: Rapid solidification of a eutectic high-entropy alloy will decrease eutectic lamellar spacing.
Rapid solidification will promote a more refined, interconnected lamellar structure.
Conventionally cast eutectic HEAs exhibit a coarse lamellar two-phase microstructure under standard cooling rates.
Cooling rates above approximately 10^3 K/s can provide the proposed refined eutectic structure.
The simultaneous improvement is expected when eutectic spacing is reduced to the sub-micron range.
Excessive residual stress or amorphization would prevent or undermine the proposed improvement.
Refinement increases the density of phase boundaries.
The increased density of phase boundaries impedes dislocation motion.
The refined phase-boundary network can accommodate plastic deformation.
Reduced lamellar spacing raises strength through a Hall–Petch-type obstruction of dislocation flow.
Improved phase connectivity facilitates more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation delays localized failure.
Rapidly solidified eutectic HEAs will have higher yield strength than conventionally cast specimens under identical test conditions.
Rapidly solidified eutectic HEAs will have higher ductility, evidenced by higher fracture strain, than conventionally cast specimens.
The proposed strength and ductility improvements are limited to room-temperature tests at standard laboratory strain rates.
The magnitudes of the strength and ductility improvements are not yet determined.
The critical cooling rate required for optimum eutectic spacing is not yet determined.
